utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Start again, if you would, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 57, in paragraph 8 of your statement you say that your commander, and I'm not going to mention his name because we're trying not to have you identified, so your commander while your unit was staying at this particular place where you were supposed to be before you went to Erdut, your commander said that there were over 3.000 Croatian MUP members there and that you were in for a serious clash; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you claim that that information was not correct and that you were told this only to be intimidated. Is that right? Is that what you feel today as well?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think. That's what I feel. 3.000 is an enormous figure. It's more than an infantry brigade. I don't think that there could have been that many MUP forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You think there couldn't have been that many forces, but tell me, as a professional soldier, are soldiers' lives in war saved by warnings in terms of numbers of the enemy and the necessity to exercise caution? Perhaps this had to do with stepped-up caution, this information that your commander had.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible. As I say, first and foremost, I am sure that it wasn't that particular figure. It is quite certain -- quite possible, rather, that he wanted to achieve the effect that you are talking about, namely that people should exercise utmost caution in order to preserve their lives. However, I'm saying that this had a different effect; people were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell me, how many of them were there, then, in your estimate? Because you say there were 3.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were a couple of hundred of them. Three hundred, in my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you explained awhile ago that it was quite possible that such information was given to you in order to exercise caution and to save soldiers' lives, at any rate, that information was not given with ill intentions. I assume that it was in the interest of saving people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be the judge of that, whether there were any ill intentions, as you said. I don't know, but I just know that the effect was very bad on the reserve force, very bad, and I said that to the subordinates at the company meeting. I said precisely what you said just now, sir, that people have to be cautious. I didn't say then, no, don't worry this is impossible, et cetera. I said that this was the orders we got from the superior command, and then the problems became even greater. People were simply frightened, if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can understand that. But this information was not ill intentioned, not in any way. It wasn't given in order to score propaganda points but in order to step up caution.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said from this distance, I cannot assess -- but, well, let's put it that way, yes. There shouldn't be any ill intention involved. I don't see any ill intention, but my comment had to do with the effect that I referred to, namely that people were truly terrified and frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't think there was any ill intention there. In paragraph 10 you refer to a group of volunteers that arrived, and among them you recognised an acquaintance of yours. I'm not going to mention his name now because you are a protected witness. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. That is paragraph 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at that time, as far as you know, he was an official of --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the Serb Radical Party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's not that I am familiar with this. I know. I quite simply know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's what you state here. And you say they were moving towards Prigrevice where the centre was of some movement of theirs, from where they were illegally transferred to Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. At that time I did not know any details about this centre, but later on a great deal was written about this centre in the newspapers. Interviews were given, et cetera. But at that time, I knew about it only superficially on the basis of a few sentences I heard from this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about interviews. I'm just trying to get you to confirm or deny the information I have, namely, according to the information I have, the Serb Radical Party gave volunteers for the JNA and later for the Territorial Defence. Did they join the JNA and the TO as volunteers or did they have some formations of their own? My information is that they gave volunteers to the JNA and the Territorial Defence. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information, as I mentioned, I think, in this paragraph 10, is -- this is a quotation: "We are going to the other side before you to help you, to prepare for your arrival." They did go. That's a fact. First to Prigrevice and then to Borovo Selo. And they joined the Territorial Defence there. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A fact. That was at the very beginning of the conflict in Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. That's the date. It was around the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means when they went there to join the Territorial Defence they had nothing to do with the JNA or any authorities in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that can be seen from this paragraph 10, and on the basis of some reactions here, they had nothing to do with us then. They had no connections with us. I think that this can be seen from my statement. As a matter of fact, I got into trouble because they stopped by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 and paragraph 12, you say that on the 25th of July, 1991, late in the evening, the area of Erdut, Daljske Planine, the Marinovci farm, and the water plant building were heavily shelled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've said, it seems that these targets were engaged for no reason whatsoever. I'm asking you this because you claim that the radio and television, in connection with this attack, said that this was response to numerous mortar fire provocations from these positions, and it's my understanding that you are saying there was no such mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any such mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On which date was your unit positioned for combat for that attack there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to clarify this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On which date did you reach this particular combat position?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of July we arrived in the broader region. The beginning of July, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You targeted, as you say, for no reason the Dalj heights and these other targets.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the end of July. And what you know from that moment when you arrived until the moment of the attack, there were no operations from the other side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you offer the possibility that they were there before you came?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That JNA targets were engaged.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my unit established the position there at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before your unit came, was there any mortar fire coming from that area and affecting that area there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know what happened before that. You cannot say whether there was or wasn't any mortar fire before that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know anything about mortar fire before or after that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say that you don't know, then you cannot preclude the possibility of there having been fire before that. I don't see why anybody would invent that kind of thing if it never happened, because mortar fire is not something that can be a secret.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I said. I would have had to know about this. That is a very public thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very public thing. And that is what was said, that there was mortar fire coming from there. I assume that nobody could have claimed that it was coming from there if there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that there wasn't any mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go over this. You have heard what the witness has said. Arguing with him is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, it says that on the 27th of July, you received a written order from your command, and in it it says that upon reaching the march objective, separate the warring sides on a particular line.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we discussed that at the previous hearing. I think that we discussed that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We covered it completely. And there's no doubt that it contained only that objective; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To separate the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated here. It can be seen right here. That was the official part that we studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, I'm not asking you to repeat everything that we concluded last time, but we're talking about these two sides. Was it the ZNG on one side and the Territorial Defence, the Serb Territorial Defence on the other side?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically the MUP of Croatia. I don't know whether the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, was formed somewhat later, but usually we used the term the members of the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the other side there were the local territorials?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local population, the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the local population.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was your objective to separate these two warring sides?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this order, that was the objective, to separate the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was a clearly stated military objective, why you entered the area?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on these orders. Yes. It is quite clear. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) then stopped the column that you were moving in before crossing the Danube, and he gave you final instructions to take good care of yourself and the men and to carry out this objective.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to ask you not to mention any names. Please. I have the status of a protected witness. You've just mentioned the colonel's name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he was not in your unit. That is why I think that he is beyond --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. He was the second person in my chain of command in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's stop. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this section can no doubt be dealt with in open court, because you say that this machine-gun fire that we discussed did not come from the positions of the MUP of Croatia but from the positions of the JNA. Is that right, Mr. C-057?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this statement after this event, but had I given it in 1992, 1993 -- I mean, whenever I talked about this, I was sure that the gunfire was coming from the MUP positions in the forest. I was deeply convinced of that. In this context, I never would have said otherwise had this man not come. I did not socialise with him personally that much, but he hinted that he wanted to talk to me about something that was bothering him terribly, and then he told me about this. And it was only then that I found out. So it was much later. This man is alive and well, thank goodness. So if there is anything controversial, I'm going to make an additional statement. I don't see why he would make up a nebulous story. I believe that he did not lie to me. Well, this is the comment I made here anyway in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-057, you yourself used the word "nebulous story" yourself a minute ago, and the story consists of the following: That gunfire was opened from JNA positions.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, you can see it here. That's what is written here, how it was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he give you some explanation? It is not possible that it could have come from JNA positions. You were an officer then. Could gunfire be opened from JNA positions against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know at least what the possible is and what actual life is. Very often we were given one kind of orders and other things happened. We discussed it at the last sitting. This is a detail which may be important for this Court, so if it is, I can give his details. I do not think he lied. Knowing him, I don't think he lied. He's not that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you? Why was gunfire opened then? Did they think that the enemy was there or did they target you intentionally?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that they shot at us intentionally. That's why this is an interesting detail. I would not have mentioned it if it was mistaken gunfire. That happens in any army. It also can happen in any army, that there is friendly fire coming from the same positions. And he talked to me then. He told me this story. It's not that we particularly socialised before that. You know what it's like when somebody first comes to see you. He came and brought some coffee, came with his wife, we had a few drinks, and he said that he had a story to tell me. And he told me this story and I looked at him the way you're looking at me right now, but knowing the way the situation was then, it wasn't that I was that surprised; anything was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you destroyed, demolished, one Croatian house in Erdut owned by an official of the HDZ. That's paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They called it secretary of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say you did it on the orders of your commander; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a verbal order that he gave you to demolish that house or was it written order?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that a messenger on a motorbike brought me that order, a verbal order, because the two of us were on the opposite ends of that settlement, and I was given that order. This verbal order was conveyed to me by a messenger on a motorbike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to understand this, because I don't know about this event. I'm only looking at your statement, and I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 16 where you say that, "Immediately afterwards, the order arrived from the command to the effect that not a single house should be demolished." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it must have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that house was destroyed. The command must have noticed it, and then the order came not to demolish any more houses.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in my statement. It might have been an arbitrary order given by my commander which was immediately revoked by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you intervene later? Did you discuss it with the superior command? How come you destroyed that house? Because they gave you orders not to destroy any houses.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After demolishing that one, I didn't destroy any other houses. You don't discuss orders. The other order came very quickly after I destroyed that one. So I stopped demolishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, 17, you say that you searched on that day a facility of the MUP of Croatia which was part of the Erdut winery, and you say that you found huge quantities of military equipment and a batch of personal documents, IDs. Would that confirm what your superior officer had told you at the outset, namely, that there is a large number of members of the MUP of Croatia in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It confirms the assumption I stated earlier, that there were about a few hundred of them, because that was the holding capacity of that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you find that weaponry?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find the weaponry, although we kept looking for it, my partner and I who did the search. We wanted to find Kalashnikovs or of Hungarian or Romanian make, but we only found parts of equipment. And I said parts of what? Parts of the US Thomson submachine-gun and cleaning kits for the Slovenian sub-machine-guns made by the Gorenje factory. And we noted because it was curious that the Slovenians had started manufacturing sub-machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I seem to remember something like that, that Gorenje did produce some machine-guns. In paragraph 18 it says that only about 10 per cent of the population remained the village, of Serb ethnicity; otherwise, it was abandoned, that village.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those people that remained were mainly elderly people?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all Croat inhabitants had left the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them. There was this couple, this married couple that I mentioned somewhere. They were younger people, relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They stayed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left later or they went missing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you found, when you came, only 10 per cent of the population in that village, whereas the other residents, mainly of Croat ethnicity, had left. That was before you entered that village; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The residents had left the village before we came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The reason for that was that they were afraid of the impending battles.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the shelling had an adverse effect, and they must have been afraid. They had left, I suppose, because they were afraid. Otherwise, they would have stayed. I'm only speaking about what we found in that village on the day we captured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, nobody expelled them from the village. They were afraid of upcoming conflicts. You didn't drive them out.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't drive anybody out. I'm describing the situation as we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I suppose -- do you know by any chance what was normally the ratio of Croat and Serb population of that village? Because I suppose some Serbs must have also left after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is really advisable for me to give such estimates, but I believe the ratio was 70 to 30, or maybe 75 to 25 in favour of the Croat population. And please, take this with a grain of salt because this is a very rough estimate. I'm making this estimate based on the size of the cemetery, not a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will take it with a grain of salt, but you as a soldier must understand that if somebody is fleeing out of fear from shelling, which is what you said yourself, I suppose that this fear must have been shared by both parts of the population. Why would Serbs not be afraid of the shelling? Why would they not flee?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very clear from my statement what happened. Very few residents of that village stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those people who stayed, if they were elderly, were those who found it hard to run away.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed to look after their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must ask you one question which the witness might consider as identifying, Mr. May, but I want one thing cleared up. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the village that we have been talking about, you say the local Serbs had M-48 rifles and sub-machine-guns, M-53. Those were weapons that the JNA was not using. So these were weapons of the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were weapons of the Territorial Defence. However, I think it is a good thing to mention here that in the late 1980s, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence issued an order that all the depots of the Territorial Defence should be placed under JNA command. I remember that very well. This was in the late 1980s. It was done in two ways; either entire depots were taken from the -- by the JNA for safeguarding, or weapons were simply taken out of these TO depots and put into storage at JNA barracks. I'm sure that this order can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It had to do with all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I learned from the media -- I read an interview of that Martin Spegelj, that former JNA general, and he also mentions that order, and he says that there was some kind of a mistake, that a certain number of rifles were simply forgotten, and they welcomed these rifles, especially at the initial stage of the establishment of the National Guards Corps. And I know of that order because this was in peacetime, and I, as an officer, escorted some of these groups that transferred the weapons from one place to another; explosives, weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that this had to do with the defence of a village that was predominantly Serb populated, can you say a bit more precisely who they were defending themselves from?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence of the village was organised in the following way: They did not allow MUP forces to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although there had been no skirmishes. The entire problem I am aware of in this connection has to do with the following: They did not allow ambulances to pass through that village as they were driving to Osijek after our bombings. So then they had to transport their wounded along the Drava and Danube rivers by boats to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to hurry because my time will run out. Tell me, please, in Dalj - and you mentioned that in paragraph 24 - you found the members of some volunteer unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I found two. There at the entrance. They had come to get some meat from a deep freezer or something like that. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were friendly to you and that they were under the command of the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I spent about 10 or 15 minutes chatting to them there. They came at the period when there was no electricity. So since there were a lot of volunteers in Borovo Selo, they wanted to get the meat out of the deep freezer so that it wouldn't go bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they came for the meat.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these volunteers were not within the JNA at the time, and they were not under the command of some JNA unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were within the defence of Borovo Selo, part of the defence of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo. Volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, your own reservists, and there were some there no doubt, I assume that you had some reservists in your unit as well, did they loot any abandoned houses or any other facilities in the villages that you passed through?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the question. The witness also said that he could not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? How did you allow them to do that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody allowed them to do that, nobody. It's not only I. Other officers also did not allow this. They tried to ban it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that precisely for stopping such activities a military police was brought in?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I say your reservists, your unit, did anybody steal anything, any person who was within your unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not somebody; I think a lot of people were involved in looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to arrest them, punish them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I threatened to court-martial all of them, and I said that I'd search the entire unit. And I said that if I found anything on anyone, that I would certainly report that to the superior command. This military police unit that came was composed of reservists, so when they were supposed to search for these stolen goods, they warned them beforehand. They'd say, for example, that tomorrow at 5.00 they would be searched, so if they had anything that had been looted, they should hide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this. This is theft from abandoned facilities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were looking for valuables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Theft from abandoned houses. So it's not that they were seizing anything from people. They were -- they were taking this from abandoned houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). Later on, I went along with the military police unit to provide security for them because they were also breaking and entering into houses because they believed that there could be members of the MUP inside. And then the reservists came, and they took objects that they thought they might need. To the best of my ability and using all the powers I had then, I fought against this, but these mechanisms were not in place. The military police themselves would tell these people, "We're going to come and search you, and you can hide your stolen goods." So they say, "See, you had no need to accuse us of this kind of thing," and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I assume that since we've clarified that during the first part, that you also cautioned your soldiers in terms of the Geneva Conventions and how civilians should be treated and possible prisoners of war. I imagine that was your duty.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to orders, because I had to issue the same kind of order. That was the logical sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When entering Aljmas - these are paragraphs 30 and 31 - again you found a completely deserted village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen from the statement. Tell me once again, what is the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say something why this village was completely deserted? What were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a Croatian village. The population had abandoned it after our bombing in late July. They got onto boats and went to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now in paragraph 32 you talk about some unit of a certain Captain Kole. Is this again a volunteer unit or a paramilitary unit? What is this? Because I see further on in your statement that a major - and I am not going to mention his name, but I assume this is a JNA major - you informed this major of their presence, and he said that they should be arrested if they showed up again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a self-established group, a self-styled group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A self-established group and a self-styled captain. This was not a regular unit and he was not a proper captain?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were four or five pals from Dalj, and they had some uniforms sewn for them. There were never such uniforms before or later. And they also made some berets in very striking colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very intensive red or pink or something like that. Well, whatever. But what was this all about? I asked my subordinates to patrol the village, and then they told me that these people had arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when you informed the major, the major said if they show up again, arrest them.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I caught them, actually when my subordinates informed me about this, I caught them with a vehicle. I mean, I am not going to lie or anything, but they had a vehicle and they had bottles of gas inside. And since they were rather arrogant, and I said, "What kind of captain are you? Where are you from?" They said they were from the Territorial Defence of Dalj and they needed this for their headquarters, and I said, "Well, I'll inform my command about this." And I did inform this major, but then he had already known about them. He actually laughed and he said, "Oh, he's showed up again." And he said, "Well, I'm going to arrest him if I see him again, and you arrest him if he shows up again," and that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted you to clarify that, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never showed up again. Well, it's not that I threatened to arrest him, but I did say that I would inform the superior command, and that's where the story of the arrest came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when Sarvas was taken, you say that a JNA aircraft was gunned down. Who gunned it down?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you entered Sarvas, you found members of the local Territorial Defence there who had already entered the village, and also members of the engineering unit who were de-mining the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So there were mines placed throughout the area by the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. At that time, I came across -- or, rather, not I but a vehicle behind me got off the asphalt road and there was a booby-trap there. Fortunately, no one was wounded, and also the vehicle itself was not damaged, and that is why we had to get rid of the mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who took Sarvas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took Sarvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-October, as you say here in paragraph 37, your unit in concert with other JNA units carried out an unsuccessful attack against Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One of your reservists got killed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the attack unsuccessful because the enemy was stronger?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enemy was not stronger. In my opinion, the attack was not prepared properly and not planned properly. I did not take part in it, but as far as I know, it was an ill-conceived attack and also the units were not engaged properly, and that is why it failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 38 -- I'm sorry. I've already asked you this. We've gone through that, so let me try to cut things short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to the death of General Bratic who was then replaced by General Andrija Biorcevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the corps commander who was killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how great the losses were sustained by the JNA in all these clashes that were taking place in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the unit involved. I've already said that during the last session. From the 2nd until the 18th, I had 27 casualties altogether, persons killed and wounded. So that meant 30 per cent losses within my unit. These are losses that I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are very high losses. They would be considered very high under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Losing a single man is too much, but this was a great loss, and I made every effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 50, you actually say that you sustained major losses because of strong mortar fire and fire coming from hand-held rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me the paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time over trying to find this paragraph. There was strong gunfire coming in, anti-armour sniper fire, gunfire, very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 57, let us just get one thing clear: You were up against a very strong and well-equipped enemy. You are talking about strong gunfire, firing coming from sniper rifles, hand-held rocket launchers and so on.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat once again: It's not that they were that strong; they were well organised, and their gunfire was very precise. But -- yes, well, I will agree. It was strong gunfire, yes. It's enough to have two mortars that are properly engaged and then this means that there will be great losses. I'm talking about the pontoon bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on you saw the local Serbs returning, those who had fled from Luzac beforehand?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't know which paragraph this is in, but I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 58, you say that as soon as they came back to the village, they set up a prison for captured members of the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were members of the MUP there, too, but I think that their Croat neighbours who were not members of the MUP were imprisoned too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone about what you found out? Did you take any measures?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I held my positions, and my superior command was in that very same village. The command followed me right into the village. I was not at the village, I did not stay there, and the headquarters were only three houses away from that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 60. Since you say that a certain commander appeared.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention his name now, because you cautioned us against that awhile ago. And he asked what was going on and what the targets were, and you said that he could shoot wherever he wanted to since there were a great many targets. Is that what you said to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said, "What is the most important target to be engaged?" And since everything was targeted, everything was a target, and I told him he could target whatever he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but if I understood you correctly, you said there were a great many targets. Therefore, there were many military targets on the enemy side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be quite specific. These are factories. That position in front of me consisted of factories, but they were used for opening fire against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was soldiers over there.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is shooting coming from there, it's a military target.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I've stopped the microphone. This must be your last question. You've gone over time as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. That's quite right. I've gone beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But could you just tell me one more thing, Mr. 57: When I say "you," I'm not referring you to personally, I'm referring to members of the JNA. So all of you targeted military targets only. You opened fire at military targets only; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything we thought was a military target, that we assessed to be a military target. It didn't always have to be a military target, but, yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness C-057, I should like to ask you for a couple of clarifications.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I leave the courtroom for a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I should appreciate it if you would provide the Court with some further explanations regarding those two orders dated the 1st July and the 27th July, 1991, and the three paragraphs in your statement that deal with these, tabs 4 and 5. I don't think it will be necessary for you to consult them. If you need to, I will ask that they be shown to you. Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, in the beginning of your examination-in-chief, insisted that you explain the term used in the order of the 1st of July, namely "internal enemy." Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: At that moment on the 1st of July when this marching order was given, was there an ongoing clash between the Territorial Defence of Slovenia and the Yugoslav People's Army preceded by the takeover of national borders with Austria and Italy?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war in Slovenia was taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It lasted for about ten days. If it started on the 25th or the 26th of June, it was still not in progress on that 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it lasted ten days, it was ongoing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It started four or five prior. Just answer my questions. In your understanding as a soldier, this takeover of national borders, did it constitute a breach of territorial integrity and sovereignty of our country? Was that the reason for the response of the JNA, among other things?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation was mounted to take back the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you remember that on the 27th of June, that is a few days before the 1st of July, Slovenia and Croatia, that is their parliaments, proclaimed their independence, in breach of the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it happened even earlier, in May, but my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in this context, this term the "internal enemy" on which the Prosecutor insisted, in the military sense and in every sense of the Serbo-Croatian language meant the person who was violating the territorial integrity of the country and its constitutional system?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the oath that you gave meant precisely that you were to protect the sovereignty and the constitutional order of the country from external and internal enemies, like in this case.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if we proceed from this order of the 1st of July, 1991, under tab 4, which order was geared at preventing inter-ethnic conflict.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so. There is no dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it was precisely the moment when the most intensive inter-ethnic conflict already existed in Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So these orders were worded nicely, but there was a totally different verbal order. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean then that although the order said "preventing inter-ethnic conflict," the actual order was to provoke inter-ethnic conflict, if I understood you correctly, because you said the verbal order was different.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was not conceived in the way you seem to suggest. The order was conceived as to suggest that all Croats are enemies, being Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, may I advise you to put a pause between the answer and your question, and not to turn on your microphone while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. This is not the first time you are warning me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the second order now, which is under tab 5. 6.3. You discussed it as well. Point 6.3 is where it says that during action, strictly respect the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Now, if you say that there was a written order like this, was there also a verbal order on the 27th of July not to respect the Geneva Conventions and the laws and customs of war? Was that really an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course nobody gave such an order not to observe Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this connection, please have a look at only three paragraphs. First of all, 95. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "In response to a question by Investigator Dzuro whether I knew about a case of an indictment being raised in Serbia in the period from 1991 until today for war crimes against civilians committed in Eastern Slavonia in 1991, 1992, I hereby reply that I have not heard of a single such case." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, find paragraph 85. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, and I'm quoting your words again: "I included everything mentioned above in my detailed written report which I concluded with a comment that the events should be resolved positively as soon as possible because they were a disgrace to the JNA." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "I made my report in one copy which I handed in. I did not make a copy for myself so that I no longer have the text of the report." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you added: "However, I still have the notebook." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we may go back to paragraph 58. In that paragraph, in the middle, it says -- when you speak about an event involving ears being cut off a Croat prisoner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, I would be very grateful if we could go into private session for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, in your last sentence, you said: "I did not inform anyone of this." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a completed sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please rest assured that I will ask you about that as well. I'm just asking you for the time being. You didn't inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you knew both the name and surname of a person who perpetrated something of this kind, and yet you did not inform anyone.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but my superiors were only a few steps away in the same place where it all took place. I'm just describing something that was perpetrated, a completed act.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then you say in paragraph 95 that you were not aware of anyone being indicted of such crimes. How could anyone be indicted if no one reports these crimes?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very logical question. Nobody can be held responsible, indeed, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the Judges?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you just say, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges how come that you did not report a terrible thing like this so that the person responsible could be brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that prison was located in the immediate vicinity of my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in the paragraph 85, which I just quoted, you said you made a detailed report on the disgrace inflicted on the JNA. How can you then explain to the Judges that a horrific event like this was not made part of that report?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made my report on specific orders concerning specific events. The event you just quoted in paragraph 58 is a totally different event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now explain this second part of sentence: "I did not inform anyone about it because I had already received instructions earlier not to restrain them." Can you tell me how you did that, in private session?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received those instructions indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But tell me from whom, the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose name and surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you received instructions not to rein in such occurrences like these ears cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's finish this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to Exhibit tab 5, the marching order of 27th of July, 1991, both Mr. Milosevic and my colleague Mr. Tapuskovic referred you to the sentence in paragraph 6.3, namely the strictly respected provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Did your superior command, before going into action, stress this point in oral briefings?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing like that was emphasised. I received that order in written form, and nothing was said verbally about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said here during your testimony, and also it is in your written statement, that violations of the Geneva Conventions did occur. Was the JNA command, including your superiors, aware of crimes being committed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they take any steps to enforce the observation of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few steps, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When discussing the newspaper article, tab 7, with Mr. Milosevic, you referred to the Serb population being afraid. In your conversations with the local Serb population, did they indicate to you that the Croatian MUP had persecuted or mistreated them? I mean the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They basically told me that they had no problems with the MUP but they were terribly afraid of them. They had had negative experience with such persons during the Independent State of Croatia, during the Second World War, and they were afraid that this kind of thing would happen again, but they did not have any specific problems, the local Serbs. They had not been molested in any way, at least in the area that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the diagram for the attack of Luzac, Mr. Milosevic spoke with you about Arkan's unit being under the command of your battalion. To engage Arkan and his men in this attack under the JNA command, was this decision made by the battalion command or was this decided within the joint command comprised of the corps and the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this decision was made at a higher level. Corps command, that's the level where the decision was passed on concerted action, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic mentioned Arkan and his people were blended into the battalion. How would you, in military terms, qualify the relation between Arkan and the battalion, and what was the relation between Arkan and the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to the question put by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It was not properly put. I commented upon the diagram that the witness made and from which it can be seen that this unit consists of the local Territorial Defence and this Serb Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan. It was a company-level unit, and it consisted of territorials and these volunteers. That is to say that he did not blend into the unit -- or, rather, he did not interfere with the unit in any way, but this unit was part of a larger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us not waste time by going over the argument again. The witness can answer the question, which was properly put, to this extent: In military terms, how would he describe the relationship between Arkan and the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arkan was integrated into the Tactical Group for attacks. It was his unit that was an integral part of the Tactical Group for attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic today -- in relation to Erdut and the mortar fires coming from the Croatian side, you said that there was no mortar fire coming from the Croatian side. My question would be, as Mr. Milosevic suggested, it may have occurred before you arrived there with your unit. Was your formation the first JNA unit that arrived there in that region on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first unit of the JNA that concentrated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic spoke with you about the inter-ethnic tolerance in your unit at that time, and he proposed to you that the JNA, during your service, had a Yugoslav orientation and did not display any discrimination against any ethnicity, and you in your answer did not endorse this. Did the JNA, during your participation in the events, protect the Croatian population at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat that yet again. That has been discussed at this session, and it was also discussed at the previous session. The oral orders we received were that the Croat population were Ustashas, that even the pets and animals were Ustashas. And I'm not the only officer who received this order, there were at least five of us, and that was the general position, regardless of this order that is insisted upon and that I handed in. That was the position, that all these people were Ustashas and that we should take care. I don't know how one measures the degree of being an Ustasha, but I'm just telling you what the facts are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the JNA, during your time in Croatia, at any point in time side with any party to the conflict? I mean, Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-057 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serb side was closer to us theoretically and practically because it was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. The Serb side was our ally. I don't know what to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C-057, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. If you'd wait a moment until the blinds come up. Yes. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to begin your testimony by stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or if I could ask the Chamber for a number or number to be assigned to a binder of exhibits, the binder containing 13 exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 608, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I might state for the record, tabs 1 and 2 of the binder are prior statements of the witness. Tabs 3 through 10 are attachments that were -- or documents that were attached to the original statements. Tab 11 is a copy of the transcript of Mr. Tihic's previous testimony in another case in the Tribunal, and the remaining exhibits, 12 and 13, are exhibits that were introduced during the course of those prior proceedings. Could I ask that the witness be shown tab 1, ask that he first be shown an English copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I know that you do not read English, but could I ask you to look through the pages of that document and ask you, do you recognise your initials at the bottom of each of those pages?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review the translation of that statement into your own language?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that you take a look at the English copy at tab 2, and ask you again, are those your initials at the bottom of each of those pages?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review the translation of that statement into your own language?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the attachments that are included on tabs 3 through 10, did you have an opportunity to review those and are those the attachments that were made and referenced in your original statements?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after having reviewed the statements and the attachments attached thereto, are there any material inaccuracies to those statements or any corrections that you need to draw the Chamber's attention to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: There are no special corrections. Perhaps there are some imprecisions in certain places, errors that are insignificant in surnames, but nothing essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after having reviewed them and now being a sworn witness, do you verify the truth and accuracy of those two prior statements, aside from these minor inconsistencies with respect, or minor inconsistencies that you say are not of essential quality to your testimony here before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, is the type of correction or inconsistency that you're talking about things such as the misspelling of the name of your neighbour of yours who does not feature in any substantive way in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, my neighbour whose last name is Pavlovic, his name was not written correctly. It says Pisarevic. But from the context of the entire statement, it could be seen that it is Pavlovic, because I did not have a neighbour by the name of Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender tabs 1 through 10 of Exhibit 608 into evidence pursuant to Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could read a brief summary of what is contained both in those statements and in a portion of the transcript which has been already admitted into evidence pursuant to a previous ruling of the Court. The witness was the president of the SDA in Bosanski Samac at the start of the war. He testifies about his arrest and detention at the police building in Bosanski Samac and his interrogation and beating suffered whilst there. He will also -- his testimony also includes a description of the treatment of other detainees held at the Bosanski Samac Territorial Defence building. Approximately on the 26th or 27th of April, 1992, he testifies about being taken to the JNA barracks in Brcko. He gives evidence about his detention there and the presence of Arkan's soldiers and Red Berets in Brcko at that time. He says that at the time it was clear to him that the paramilitary forces were cooperating with the JNA and that even some JNA soldiers appeared to be afraid of the paramilitary troops. He gives evidence about an interview that he was required to give to TV Novi Sad in Serbia. He testifies about the outbreak of the war in Brcko and his transfer on the 1st or 2nd of May to the JNA barracks in Bijeljina. He further testifies about interrogations and beatings by the JNA soldiers there. The witness was subsequently forcibly transported by helicopter to Batajnica in Serbia where he was detained. He was guarded by JNA young recruits. He testifies about his treatment there. He was subsequently transported to Sremska Mitrovica prison in Serbia. He testifies about the commander of the camp, a regular JNA soldier, and about beatings suffered at the hands of soldiers there. I will ask Mr. Tihic a few particular questions that are of particular relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, the Chamber has before it a very detailed account of the events in Bosanski Samac. Can I ask you at this time to describe or to list the names of the units of paramilitary or special forces that you were aware of from Serbia that were present in the takeover of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: These are special units that were called the Red Berets, Arkan's men, the Grey Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you learn when the unit that you've described as the Red Berets, did you learn when they first arrived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, before the attack on Bosanski Samac, perhaps ten or 15 days prior to the attack, a client of mine came to see me, because I had been working as a lawyer, and he said to me that the Red Berets were transferred to Batkusa by helicopter and that they were making trouble, if I can put it that way, in the village over there because they had beaten up a patrol, a Serb patrol that was on guard duty vis-a-vis the neighbouring Croat village, because they sat in a cafe with a Croat patrol, and they socialised. They thought that this was not right, and that's why they beat them up. So then they complained about that, and also they were cutting the hair of people who had long hair in the village. They were molesting women, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As best you're able, can you fix for the Chamber the date or the approximate date upon which these Red Berets would have arrived by helicopter in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: If Samac was attacked on the 17th, then they were there ten or 15 days before that, so it was perhaps the beginning of April 1992. These persons and similar persons appeared in town wearing civilian clothes. We noticed that there were people who were speaking the Ekavian dialect, who were not speaking Bosnian the way people talk in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of April when the Red Berets would have arrived in Bosanski Samac, prior to that, had there been any outbreak of violence or any trouble in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The Red Berets came to a village near Bosanski Samac, about ten kilometres away from Bosanski Samac. The name of the village is Batkusa. Well, the atmosphere in Bosanski Samac was the way it was. It's a town on the border, and that was probably the only way out of Bosnia, across the Sava river. There was tension but people lived normal lives to the extent possible at that time. It's not that people were killed or wounded, but there were verbal conflicts. And also there were some cases in which mines were placed, but people did not suffer any injuries due to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the television screen before you, and I'm going to ask that Exhibit 349, tab 4 -- and I would note that that's a correction from the summary, the summary incorrectly notes this exhibit as tab 5 -- it is 349, tab 4, that I would ask you to look at, and I would ask you, do you recognise this patch?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan's Tigers, that is the patch of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 349, tab 16. I'd ask that be placed on the screen at the same time as the other exhibit. Now, I want to draw your attention not to the entirety of this patch but to the symbol the cross with the four Ss or reverse Cs, in the left-hand corner. Did you ever see that insignia or that portion of this insignia in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see such insignia. It is well known because the letters S, written in Cyrillic, are turned in the opposite direction, quite different from all the others that were exhibited at that time. The Ss are in the completely opposite direction as compared to all the others. And one of them who had these patches said that the concord that no longer existed between and among the Serbs was no longer there because the Serbs were -- had turned their backs to each other, whereas now that they changed the insignia, the Ss were facing each other, as it were, and that is why Serbs would live in greater concord because they would face each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: President Tihic, the more typical symbol with the Ss, Cyrillic Ss, is that reflected in the upper portion of the Arkanovci patch on the left-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is an atypical patch. That's why I remembered it in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you to describe for the Chamber the interaction between these units of the Red Berets, Arkanovci, and the other units from Serbia. Could I ask you to describe their interaction with the local military in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, those special units, the Specials, as we called them, they were masters of that war, masters of life and death. The local Serb units, and even the JNA units, were much more tolerant towards us. They were willing to make allowances to let us go, but these people wouldn't let them. Everybody was afraid of them. I know a couple of Serb policemen who were beaten up just because they had been tolerant to us. Even the local Serbs were afraid of them, and the troops were afraid of them. And while I was in Bosanski Samac, they beat people. They were the only ones who beat people. Occasionally an extremist from among the Serbs would join them and would gain more importance thereby. However, the majority of local Serbs were embarrassed because of the position that we had been put in, at least during the time that I spent in Bosanski Samac, the ten days. They beat us so bad that the local commander from Bosanski Samac called the JNA and asked him to pull us all out because we would die from the beatings otherwise. And one of these units of the JNA was afraid that the specials who had gone on a mission somewhere would come back, in which case they wouldn't be able to pull us out, and they were afraid of clashing with them, at least as far as Bosanski Samac is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, your -- both your statements and your prior testimony, you give a very detailed description of the crimes that you were subjected to, the many beatings and incarcerations that you suffered. Can I ask you, did you learn the names of any of the people who committed these crimes against you personally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: We knew their nicknames. We didn't know their full names. I know in Bosanski Samac there were Lucky, Musa, Lugar, Beli, Zvezdan, and they were the most vicious beaters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They looted, robbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learned the last name or the formal name of this person that you've referred to as Zvezdan?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I learnt his name. When I got out of these concentration camps in Serbia, I was in Rijeka and received a visit from my relative who was free. He told me, I heard that you had been beaten by Zvezdan. His name is actually Jovanovic. It seems that this relative of mine had known this Zvezdan in Samac. That's how I learned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did your relative from Bosanski Samac know this person Zvezdan as Zvezdan Jovanovic? Can you describe the circumstances under which he knew him.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: At that time, they spent time together Bosanski Samac. My relative said that Zvezdan used to bring him blank driver's licences and he would type in names and details, because there were many stolen vehicles and Zvezdan wanted to change the owner's name and register them. Later, they sat together in cafes and Zvezdan told him, "I beat up your relative quite a few times," meaning me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The cars that were stolen, were these cars that were taken from the Muslim and Croat population during this -- the spring and summer of 1992 in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were taken away from Muslims and Croats, and the names of the real owners would be replaced in these blank driver's licences. My relative would receive instructions from Zvezdan which name to type in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I'm going to ask you to look at portion of videotape. It's Exhibit 390, tab 1. I'm going to ask you to listen to the names of the people that introduced themselves to the accused, Mr. Milosevic, and then I'll ask you a question regarding whether you recognise the names of any of these people. I'll ask that be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is that the same name of the person who beat you while you were in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As you sit here ten years later, are you confident in your ability to recognise this person from this video, from the face?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can hardly recognise him because this recording is not very good. He seems to be wearing glasses here. Just by how tall he is, he seems to be the same person, but it's difficult for me to say whether it's really the same man. The name does correspond, but otherwise -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your prior statement and your testimony, you refer to a person by the name of Djordjevic, also known as Crni, and could I ask you to describe to the Chamber what you know about his background, what you came to know about his background and where he was from prior to the activities that he engaged in in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Earlier, as far as I know, he used to be a member of the federal police in Belgrade. For a while, from what I heard, he was in retirement, but when the war broke out, he joined the military, and he was the commander of this unit that was stationed in Bosanski Samac. Crni was their commander. I know that he even got married in Bosanski Samac, and took over the property of his bride.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --
