utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He commanded that unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, your prior testimony and statement go into great detail about what happened to you in both Brcko and Bijeljina. If I could now draw your attention to the period of time when you were taken from Bosnia and forcibly transported into Serbia. Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber how it was you were taken from Bosnia into Serbia and when that was.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: From the military barracks of the JNA in Brcko, we were transferred to the Spanac barracks in Bijeljina. I think it was on the 2nd or the 3rd of May, 1992. And two or three days after we arrived, they came and called out a couple of names. They blindfolded us and directed us to leave the building where we were put up. We walked in the direction of a helicopter. We were put into that helicopter, and inside there were already three men from Samac; Izetbegovic, Izet Izetbegovic, Dr. Keracic, and a third man.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the middle of the helicopter there was a coffin holding the body of a fighter who had gotten killed. There was one of Arkan's men and one major wearing civilian clothes. We were tied to each other, in fact handcuffed to each other. The helicopter took off. I know we flew over two rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting you but the interpreters were not able to catch the third name, the name that you mentioned after Mr. Izetbegovic. Can I ask you to repeat the name of the third individual who was taken into the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The people who were already in the helicopter were Izet Izetbegovic, Dr. Miroslav Keracic, and Anto Dragicevic. They were already inside. And the men who came with me from Grga Zubak, Anto Lucic, Anto Simovic, Dragan Lukac, Sead Mujkanovic. I think there were six of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just what relationship if any was there between Izet Izetbegovic and Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Izet Izetbegovic and Alija Izetbegovic were sons of brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you when you were describing the manner in which you were restrained in the helicopter. Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber again how it was that you were restrained while you were in that helicopter.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In the middle of that helicopter lay the coffin of that dead soldier. On the left and on the right of the coffin the nine of us sat, handcuffed to each other. Behind us was one Arkan's man and on the other was the major in civilian clothes. On the way, the Arkan's man wanted to throw us out of the helicopter, but this major - and I know that he was a major because he later interrogated us in Batajnica - would not allow that. We flew over two rivers before we landed at an airfield. I think it was Batajnica. It was Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you handcuffed in any way?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: We were all handcuffed. Handcuffed to each other. It was enough to push only one of us out the door and we would all fly out of the helicopter. I had one-half of the handcuff tied to my hand and the other half of the handcuff was tied to the next person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the person who you're describing as a member of the Arkanovci in this helicopter, how was it that you knew that he was a member of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I knew by his patch and the black cap they wore, the knit cap. They wore all the emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did -- was he handcuffed or restrained in any way while he was on that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He was the person who was guarding us. He was in charge of our security, if you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the helicopter, were you able to identify from what organisation or unit the helicopter came from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when we were going into the helicopter, we were blindfolded, and from under the blindfold you could discern that it was a JNA helicopter, but which unit it belonged to we couldn't really tell because we had to keep our heads down, and we had to keep our heads down even while we were inside. We were not allowed to look left or right or up. We just had to keep our heads down all the time. I can't tell which unit the helicopter belonged to, but it was a JNA helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, again your statement and your testimony go into great detail about your treatment in Batajnica and subsequently in Sremska Mitrovica prison, including attempts to force you to participate in the taping of a propaganda film. The final question I have for you this morning is: During your incarceration, did you have a conversation with a JNA soldier by the name of Aco Ilic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a decent kind of soldier. He was originally from Loznica. He said so himself. He had many friends among Bosnians. He helped us in Batajnica as much as he could. He would bring us biscuits, once he even brought beer. And while he was on guard, nobody was allowed to beat us. I know that sometime towards the end he left, but before that he came to say goodbye and he said he was going to the front line in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was towards the end of our stay in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he say whether he was receiving any additional benefits or additional pay for volunteering to go to the front line in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You see, besides from -- besides Aco Ilic, there were other guards who volunteered to go to Bosnia, and they said that they would be receiving the same salaries they were receiving in Serbia, but they would receive also an additional bonus for going to Bosnia. They would get a higher salary, like professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the period of your incarceration, the JNA formally withdrew from Bosnia around the 19th and 20th of May. Are you able to say whether the conversation that you had with Mr. Ilic or any of the other men was before or after the formal withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think it was after that, two or three days prior to our transfer to Sremska Mitrovica, which was on the 27th of May. I know this also because it was a time when Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted into the United Nations. This happened after the recognition, and it was later declared that the JNA was going to withdraw from Bosnia. And we were admitted into the UN on the 22nd of May, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When were you ultimately released from your imprisonment in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of August. There was a large exchange in a place called Nemetin under an agreement between Premier of Yugoslavia Panic and Gregoric. We were part of that large exchange. We were exchanged together with Croat prisoners mainly from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to cross-examine the witness. We've considered how long you should have in the light of the length of the Prosecution examination, and we conclude an hour -- one hour, three-quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to manage within that time, Mr. Tihic. I'm not sure I will, though. Mr. Tihic, in your statement, in the very beginning you say that, in addition to other statements, you made a statement just after you were exchanged in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the documents that I made here were drawings of the rooms where I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean what it says in the second paragraph: "I brought with me a document that I wrote after I was released from the camp in Serbia, and I'm giving you a copy. I felt that I was forgetting things so I wrote down names and events from my memory. That document covers events from before the election in 1990 up until the time I got out of the camp in 1992." That's what my question relates to.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you felt you were forgetting things, so you noted down events and names. I suppose it covers the period from 1990 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you still have that document today? Do you have it with you? Could I see it, perhaps, since as you say you've submitted it and I haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still have it today, and I submitted it in the trial of the Samac group. I simply wanted to note down the kind of details that tend to fade in memory, such as names, the sequence of events. I tried to write down the chronology of all that I had suffered in the several camps I've been to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I should like to have that document when it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will make an inquiry about it. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking for that document now, and as soon as we identify it, we'll notify the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, at the time of the events that you are testifying about, you discharged important functions within the SDA party in your municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I volunteered as president of the SDA party and president of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But president of the party is probably the most prominent personality in the party and in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you've been in the SDA since it was established?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the information available to me, you were an MP in the Assembly of Republika Srpska from 1996 to 2002.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in 2001, the High Representative of the international community appointed you member of the parliamentary commission for constitutional issues; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were elected president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From my information, when you were elected, you made a speech to the public and the MPs present and party members, saying that your party would work for the implementation of the provisions of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I said I would work on the implementation of Annex 4 to the Dayton Accords, and these accords have a total of ten annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is it that's so particular about Annex 4?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It envisages strengthening the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state and making them more efficient as well as creating a unified economic space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know what you mean, but do you mean a change of status of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Among other things, I believe that the entity called nowadays Republika Srpska cannot be named after one nation only because Bosnia and Herzegovina is a multinational state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The way Republika Srpska is named is up to the people of Republika Srpska to decide.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That should be decided in keeping with the constitution, and all peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be asked about it, should have a say, and there should be a consensus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a current debate. It has nothing to do with the indictment, and as far as I can see, nothing to do with this trial. So we'll go on to something else which has to do with this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With what you call "this trial," there is probably a connection of what Mr. Tihic just said, the need for consensus among peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 29897 to 29908.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the past decade since the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a state where political decision-making has been based precisely upon agreement among Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, and even personnel decisions were taken with a view to the need for equal representation.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Bosnia and Herzegovina should be a state of all the three peoples. That's the kind of Bosnia I always worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it beyond dispute that problems in Bosnia started precisely when a decision was made ignoring Serbian people for Bosnia to leave Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what the problems started. Problems, in my opinion, started because the JNA got involved in Bosnian affairs. In other words, an aggression was mounted against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbs, Croats and Muslims in Bosnia would never wage war against each other if there had been no outside interference, if there had not been involvement of special units from all sides. We as neighbours would never fight each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. If Croats from Croatia and Serbs from Serbia caused all that, how come that there had been no conflicts before the collapse of that famous Cutileiro plan which had been signed at first by Alija Izetbegovic, who then withdrew his signature, whereas Serbs and Croats accepted this plan with the proviso that Bosnia should be cantonised? Is that correct, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These are factual issues. I don't have to dwell on this any longer. Let us go back to the events that you are testifying about and your statement too. Is it correct that in 1990, among the newly established political parties - I'm referring to the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ - in the territory of your municipality some kind of political agreement was reached, or, rather, you cooperated in order to topple the communists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a parliamentary majority that elected the then-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it uncontested that the division of public offices within the municipality once you won the election, I'm referring to these three parties, was based precisely on the agreement among the three parties? You refer to that in paragraph 4 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Changes only took place in public offices, namely in economic companies changes were not carried out because there were these other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you had also been a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For how long were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was a member from the fourth grade of high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as soon as you became of age, you became a member. As early as possible; is that right? And then until 1990, all the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in fourth grade of high school, and then in paragraph 4 you say that you were not a member of the League of Communists out of conviction but, rather, because that was the way in which you could pursue your professional interests in the best way.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see in the League of Communists, practically all educated people were within the ranks of the League of Communists. The ideas advocated by the League of Communists were progressive, acceptable. They spoke of justice, equality among people. So why would I not be in the League of Communists at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not the question I'm putting to you, why you would not be a member of the League of Communists but what you said a few minutes ago here was that you became a member of the League of Communists while you were still in high school, and here you say, "I was a member of the -- member of the League of Communists before the war because it was impossible to work as a judge or lawyer if you were not."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's right too, because especially in the provinces, it was very difficult to be a judge or a prosecutor. I mean, you could not be head of a shop if you were not a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that, that you could not do anything if you were not a member of the League of Communists, because then all employees would have been members of the League of Communists, especially lawyers. I do not know of most lawyers being members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Perhaps in Bosanski Samac, so then you would be an exception, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, formally you could be a judge of the Constitutional Court without being a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you could not work as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that does not mean that a lawyer could not -- become a lawyer without being a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Perhaps that is imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you this because this is inaccurate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, lawyers were not members of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But then you wrote something -- then you wrote something that is not true. But let us go on. Is it correct that during 1991 you were also a member of the National Security Council of the SDA? Is that right? You referred to that in paragraph 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Main Board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you were a member of the National Security Council of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was not. As far as I know, such a council didn't even exist as a body, as a permanent body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You became a member of the National Council of the SDA for all of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You probably mean the Main Board of the SDA. Perhaps the translation is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that together with this Izet Izetbegovic who was mentioned here who is therefore the nephew -- or, no, the cousin of Alija Izetbegovic; is that right? That together with him, on behalf of the Muslims of Bosanski Samac, you attended a meeting at Mount Igman towards the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened at that meeting? Is that when this National Security Council of the SDA was established?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It's not that it was founded then. Various current political issues were discussed at that meeting, and towards the end of the meeting some members voiced their concern over the arming of the Serbs by the JNA. It was also indicated that Croats were receiving weapons from Croatia and that we Muslims had no weapons, and that in a way, we had remained disarmed because previously the JNA had taken the weapons of the Territorial Defence, and these two ethnic groups had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was in 1991, and is it true that at that meeting regional and municipal Crisis Staffs were first established?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was formally done at that meeting, but these Crisis Staffs were being established after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it beyond any doubt that the leadership of the SDA that you belonged to already then at the end of 1991 quite clearly opted in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. We wanted to preserve Yugoslavia as a community of equal and equitable peoples, and President Izetbegovic advocated that. However, other forces prevailed, and he could not succeed. Because we knew what a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina could mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it certain that the Serbs advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia? Is that at least beyond doubt?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not, because all other peoples wanted Yugoslavia as a community of equitable peoples, whereas Serbs, or, rather, the policy that then represented the Serbs wanted a Yugoslavia in which the Serbs would be more equitable, to say the least, in relation to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Izetbegovic -- or Mr. Tihic, don't you know that in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was established in April 1992, when you seceded and when you were internationally recognised, that that is precisely where citizens were equal and equitable and that throughout that decade there had been no ethnic discrimination whatsoever. And as a matter of fact, 70.000 Muslims fled as refugees to Serbia to seek shelter there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, and least of all do I know that they were equal. I mean, Muslims were taken out of trains and killed in this "equitable Yugoslavia" as you say. So the other day in Serbia, the perpetrators were tried, and these Muslims were taken off a train and killed. So that's that equality for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic -- Mr. Tihic, those people who were taken out were taken out of the train in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not in Serbia, and you know that full well. And you also know full well how the authorities reacted to that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how they reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It did not happen in Serbia, it happened in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After all, that is a fact that cannot be brought into question.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, if we're supposed to discuss this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not discussing the train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not going to discuss this. It seems a complete waste of time to have this sort of argument. Now, we'll hear evidence. If you've got some questions for the witness which he can deal with without argument, we'll listen to them, but otherwise we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I shall ask you to give answers that are as brief as possible to my questions. Do you know that on the 13th of January, 1991, in Bosanski Brod a meeting was held of the representatives of the HDZ of Northern Bosnia where a commission was elected with the task of talking in Slavonski Brod to the Ministers of Defence and the Interior Martin Spegelj and Josi Bojlkovic [phoen] about the arming of Bosanska Posavina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the leadership of the SDA of Sarajevo on the 11th of July, 1991 sent to the municipal representatives of the SDA a document called Instructions for Sending Candidates to the Educational Centre of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, which was signed by Secretary Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not receive that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, as the then-president of the SDA for Bosanski Samac, that on the 9th of August, 1991 - 1991, I underline - the headquarters of the SDA sent instructions regarding mobilisation, military exercises, and stating the following: That these matters have to do with their party affiliation within the municipal Secretariats of National Defence, not the federal administration. B, that they insist on the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 7th of August that recruits from the BH can serve their military term only in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia; and thirdly, that call-up papers can be addressed only by municipal authorities, not by military organs. Do you recall that and is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was the SDA that sent this document. I think that this was either a decision of the Presidency not to go and do one's military service. I think it was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina that decided that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in August the same year the arms smuggling channel was cut off, the arms that were illegally transported from Croatia to Bosnia for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your area.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember that in October 1991, the first Serb refugees started arriving from Croatia, and they were taken care of by a special commission in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I remember that. I remember that. From Slunj and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that on the 27th of November, 1991, from -- the Croatian side stopped traffic on the bridge on the Sava River spanning the two river banks, Bosanski Samac and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Possibly. Traffic would be stopped from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that on that occasion the Crisis Staff from Slavonski Brod informed the president of the Municipal Assembly in Bosanski Samac that the reason for stopping traffic was the fact that JNA units and Chetnik gangs were concentrating there? I am quoting that document. Continued quotation: On the Bosnian side and that the bridge was mined.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're not sure?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know that this kind of document was sent. I know that traffic was stopped and I knew that there were these remarks regarding the concentration of troops because they were afraid that these troops would cross over to Croatia, but as for a concrete document, letter, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But towards the end of November 1991, did a series of sabotage and diversion actions where the transmission lines were blown up in Lugovi and also Alija Fitozovic, your colleague and party comrade, had stashed away a lot of Vitezit 20, a well-known explosive, and also a diagram for carrying out those actions?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know that the transmission lines were blown up, but I don't know who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that Fitozovic had the explosives, your colleague Fitozovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know that some explosives were found in Alija Fitozovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that on the 9th of December 1991 there was a diversion using the same kind of explosives in Hranaprodukt?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how this sabotage took place, but I did know about an explosion at the Hranaprodukt company and I don't know who did that. The perpetrators were never found in any one of these cases. We thought it was done by the JNA, they thought somebody else was doing that, and that is how mutual accusations were levelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On the 23rd of December, was there yet another act of sabotage, again near Podlugovi number 182 -- no, not Podlugovi but again a transmission line. I meant Lugovi. This was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, Lugovi. There were sabotage acts of this kind; seven, eight, ten, I don't know if it was twice at Lugovi or only once but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of December -- the one I referred to just now was on the 223rd, but on the 24th of December your party colleague Alija Fitozovic, who was also an SDA official; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Executive Board, the municipal Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the Crisis Staff of Slavonski Brod he received an ID allowing him safe passage through checkpoints; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of him getting this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 26th of December the poles of the transmission -- on the transmission lines between Tuzla and Djakovo were mined and also the shop of a Serb, Janja Zubak, in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the transmission lines and Janja Zubak is not a Serb. She's a Croat and her husband, Grga Zubak, was imprisoned with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was her kiosk blown up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, her kiosk was right by the MUP, the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 10th of January, 1992, a new hand-over of explosives took place between Alija Fitozovic and Nefrid Dzananovic from Odjaci [phoen] and that a certificate to that effect was found in Fitozovic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in January 1992, a large quantity of weapons was obtained from Croatia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, January 1992.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A large quantity of arms from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that in April, just before the attack on Samac, something did come from Croatia, but January I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Before the attack on Samac, arms came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fifty automatic rifles. And that was given to the Territorial Defence Staff. And these weapons were mostly taken away when Samac was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, they were seized?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they were the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now you're talking about April, but I am dwelling on January. The 27th of January, that is the holiday of St. Sava, the chapel at the Orthodox cemetery in Bosanski Samac was blown up. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know that it was blown up, the chapel, but I don't know whether it was on the 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the -- well, Saint Sava's day was chosen because that is a big Serb holiday.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I did not know that it was exactly on that holiday but I know that it was damaged to an extent, it wasn't totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explosives were placed there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 5th of February, 1992, the bridge on the Sava River also had explosives placed on it and was partly damaged?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, partly damaged, yes, but I don't know whether it was on the 5th of February, possibly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 8th of February from the village of Donji Hasici a mortar attack was launched against the neighbouring Serb village of Skaric? This was on the same day when your associates Izet Izetbegovic and Alija Fitozovic brought ammunition and hand grenades and anti-tank mines from Slavonski Brod. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I do not know about this shelling of Skaric from Hasici. Well, you see, all these explosions that took place, there were different versions in this regard who the perpetrators were. We thought that this done by the JNA and by the Serb side in order to create a state of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about what I referred to just now in the second part of my question, about bringing in ammunition by Fitozovic and Izetbegovic, ammunition, hand grenades, anti-tank mines and so on, precisely then when this shelling of Skaric took place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it happened on that day, but I know they brought a case of ammunition, two hand grenades and I believe one anti-tank mine from Croatia. I was informed of it. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were informed of that quantity you are talking about, not a greater quantity; just one case of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who Rifat Atic is, nicknamed Rajec, owner of the Molar [phoen] coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 2nd of March he took over a delivery of a large quantity of ammunition from Slavonski Brod and that ammunition was intended for SDA units in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think you're talking about the same thing, actually, the same shipment. Atic brought this one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, the first thing happened on the 8th of February and the second case was on the 2nd of March, and it was 10.000 pieces, not just one case.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know there was one delivery only, whether it was Atic or Fitozovic who brought it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know that a receipt, 1342, was found on one of them on the 2nd of March, issued on the 2nd of March.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know that there was only one consignment. Whether it was Izetbegovic or Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the night between the 12th and 13th of March a delivery was made on two trucks secured by Namic Sulic [phoen], commander of the police from Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the meeting of the 19th of March in the Prud village, attended by Stjepan Bozanovic, nicknamed Braco, special envoy of the HDZ from Croatia; Mato Nujic, Filip Evic, Izet Izetbegovic, Vinko Dragicevic, Alija Fitozovic, and this Marko Bozanovic and yourself; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that meeting, I came towards the end only. That meeting fell through because I personally didn't want to agree, and Marko Bozanovic didn't agree either, with the establishment of a Crisis Staff where only Croats and Muslims would be included. I wanted a Crisis Staff where Serbs would be included as well. That's why this meeting fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that a Crisis Staff was set up then and a single army command where Bozanovic was the commander and Fitozovic was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't set up then because I didn't want to agree with a Crisis Staff without Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was only a proposal that you didn't accept because you were against it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I was explicitly and strongly against it, and Marko Bozanovic supported me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But how was the nucleus then formed of the 104th Brigade of the HVO? Because my information was that this meeting was the beginning of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how the brigade was set up. I was in the camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you remember that on the 25th of March, 1992, on the railway in Samac, explosives were found, the railroad had been mined?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that at that time on the 25th of March, Fuad Jasenica, Jogo, an activist of the SDA from Samac, brought from Croatia a large shipment of automatic rifles including ammunition and two launchers?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's what I mentioned as a case from April when 50 automatic rifles were brought from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There are two shipments, the beginning of March and the 25th of March. The paper found on Atic was dated the 2nd of March. He brought it across the border on the 25th of March, and we are talking about two different consignments and you know only about one of them.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know about the case of Jasenica. That weaponry was brought to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence and surrendered to them, and I know that Atic, Fitozovic, and whoever it was with them brought some weapons from Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You became president of the Crisis Staff in March; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It was a Crisis Staff that was set up within the party of the SDA, and all presidents of municipal boards were presidents of Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There were Izet Izetbegovic, Fitozovic, Nalic, and Hadzialijagic in addition to you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true at the same time that a municipal military staff was set up, headed precisely by Alija Izetbegovic, Fitozovic, Rifat Atic, Fakija Baptic [phoen], et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This Crisis Staff had a section that dealt precisely with security and organisation of defence because, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, Muslims accounted for only 7 per cent of the population, and we were concentrated in the town itself. We were concerned because we were cut off from the rest of Bosnia at a time when Serbs and Croats were getting very well armed, Serbs by the JNA and Croats by Croatia. We found ourselves in the middle, and we were thinking about what to do. We tried to organise ourselves and provide for some sort of security although it couldn't be compared to the capacities of the Serbs and Croats because they were much more numerous in municipalities and they enjoyed the support of their respective states, so that our efforts were really incomparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. Since you say that Serbs enjoyed the support of the JNA and Croats of the Croatian state, is it true that then in 1991 there was a boycott of the JNA and refusal to receive call-up papers and Muslims en masse refused to be mobilised into the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's true. In response to an appeal made by the president, Alija Izetbegovic, not to respond to call-up, young men really refused because, among other things, they were afraid of being sent to front lines in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that you excluded yourself from the JNA and then said that JNA didn't want you? You refused call-up papers yourselves. If you had stayed in the JNA, you wouldn't have taken any action against yourselves. Isn't that obvious?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: There were mostly Serbs in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were all ethnicities represented in the command.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You know that soldiers were mostly Serb, and they were commanded by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that the composition of the commanding staff was proportional to the composition of the population.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was that proportional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We need not discuss concrete data because it is available to everyone. Is it also true that one of the main objectives of those Crisis Staffs of the SDA was to arm your Muslim units in the municipalities where these Crisis Staffs existed? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you about Bosanski Samac. There were no serious units. They did not exist, and we were not able to arm them, because we accounted for only 8 per cent of the total population of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But we did note a moment ago, and we agreed, that there were at least some activities geared at arming, although you accounted for only 7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of any aggressive actions taken against army officers, barracks, their families, military facilities at the time in your area, a locality you were very familiar with regardless of whether it was strictly within the administrative borders of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know about Bosanski Samac and the surrounding area. There were no officers there, there were no barracks, there were no such actions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement you mentioned the 4th Detachment, and you call it detachment of the JNA. You claim that it was an integral part of the 17th Tactical Group commanded by Colonel Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me first, on what basis do you claim that this 4th Detachment was part of the JNA? Could it have been the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't, because Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic came and informed us in the municipality that they were part of the JNA and that similar units exist in other municipalities. We were opposed to that and we said that under the constitution, such units can only be part of the Territorial Defence, but he wouldn't hear of it and he established the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm trying to say. Is it true that it was a unit of the Territorial Defence that included both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, this 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It was a JNA unit. It was not under the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, it was part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a good moment to adjourn. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. President Tihic, may I give you the warning we give all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go on until 2.00, which should give us time to finish the evidence of this witness. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, let us clarify about this 4th Detachment. You yourself, Mr. Tihic, in paragraph 7 of your statement, speak about two of your fellow townsmen, and I'm quoting you. You say: "They organised the 4th Detachment of the JNA in Samac by recruiting civilians who had weapons. 80 per cent of the members were Serbs, but there were also some Muslims and Croats." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was organised by the JNA, the barracks in Brcko, and they were formally and in reality under their competence, and they provided them with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm quoting you here. You wrote about your fellow townsmen, that they organised the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac by recruiting civilians who had weapons. And you say 80 per cent were Serbs and the rest were Muslims and Croats, and you said yourself that Muslims accounted for only 7 per cent of the population. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The detachment was made up of people who were local residents of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 10: "Nikolic did not have legal authority to establish the 4th Detachment because only the republican authorities had competencies to do something like that." So who was it; Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Nikolic organised the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you say, that "they" organised it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You must have taken this out of context. The entirety of my statement must indicate that it was the JNA, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, who organised the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 7. In the middle of that paragraph, after mentioning all these names and their positions, you say: "They organised the 4th Detachment of the JNA within the town of Bosanski Samac by recruiting civilians with weapons. 80 per cent of the members were Serbs but there were also some Muslims and Croats." And I'm quoting you verbatim. That is what you stated.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, the entirety of my statement says that it was organised by the JNA, by Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, and the JNA provided their weapons. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They recruited civilians who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. They distributed weapons to civilians. And everybody knows where it was done; in the factory at Tekstilac. These people were invited to come there and they distributed the weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These two don't fit, together but never mind. In paragraph 9, you say that Lieutenant Colonel, or Colonel Nikolic, I'm not sure about this, it doesn't matter anyway, at a time when the JNA were still in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he would come to Bosanski Samac, talking to people about security and telling them to organise the defence of the town. However, the majority did not want the JNA to be involved in the work of the TO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It's true that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic came. He would attend sessions of the Security Council and the local community and he did not want to cooperate with the Territorial Defence. That is true. He wanted the JNA to take over all security affairs in the municipality without involving the TO, which we were opposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm quoting again from your paragraph 9: "He came to meetings discussing security, telling people to organise the defence of the town with the army, but most of the people at the security meeting did not want the army involved with the Territorial Defence." This is completely opposite to what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not true. The Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic and the entire JNA at the time ignored the TO. They didn't want any part of them, and that's why they disarmed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt. Your Honour, I'm now in possession of the statement, the English and the B/C/S version. These are personal memoirs of the witness. They were first disclosed to the accused on 21st of March, 2003. I have additional copies here to provide him. In fairness, I would point out the name of the witness isn't prominent on the document but it is mentioned in the footer, but it may not have been obvious that this was this particular witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the accused have one copy, the witness have another. And have you got a copy for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll have those produced now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is very voluminous material, as far as I can see, but I suppose Mr. Groome made a slip of the tongue when he said that it was discovered in 1993. I suppose he meant it was discovered in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. It was disclosed on the 3rd of -- I'm sorry, the 21st of March, 2003.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But not indicating the name of the witness. I really don't know how to find my way in this sea of papers, especially when names of witnesses are not indicated. But now I have no time to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, Mr. Tihic, since you say that the majority was against involving the JNA in the work of the TO, what majority are you talking about? Do you mean Muslims from the territory of Bosanski Samac? Right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I said that we wanted the JNA and the TO to cooperate, as envisaged by the legislation and the constitution. We were opposed to having the JNA as the sole guarantor of our security. Croats and Muslims were both against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say he talked about organising the defence of the town with the army but most of the people at the security meeting did not want the army involved with the Territorial Defence, this is pretty unequivocal in your statement. You say that you mean Muslims and Croats now.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I mean Muslims, Croats, and others who were against having the JNA as the sole guarantor of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why would the JNA ask to be the only guarantor if Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic came to these meetings and asked you to jointly organise the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's not what he asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that's what you wrote here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it really worked, but I'm telling you what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what you wrote. He told the people that they should organise the defence of the town with the army. That's what it says in your statement. Regardless -- all right. When you talk about Nikolic's appeal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you going to say something, Mr. Tihic, or not? If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In this connection regarding the defence of the town, from whom was the town supposed to defend itself and the surrounding area as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: There were various misgivings on various parts. The Serbs who were in town were afraid that the KOS people might come from the other side of the river, from the Croatian side, while we the Muslims who were the majority in town were afraid that the JNA, the Serb Territorial Defence could take over the town and repeat the scenario that had already taken place in Bijeljina and upstream along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the words of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic about the defence of the town. I suppose it did not mean defending the town from some Serbs who were supposed to attack it. From whom did he ask you to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic in his public speeches tried to rise above it all and treat equally both Serb forces and Croatian forces. As a representative of the JNA, he was supposed to defend us from both. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true what you say in paragraph 17, namely that members of the 4th Detachment patrolled only by night in the areas of the Bosna River and the Sava River, because that's the side from which they expected an attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that before. They feared an attack from the other side, from some Croatian village across the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this expected attack was supposed to come from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They feared that an attack might come from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13, speak about the self-defence of the Muslims. You say that it was not organised by professional soldiers, and it was meant only to fend off attacks from outside, and the problem was that the JNA had taken away all the weaponry a year before.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's true. We had some city guards who could not be very efficient in defending us, but they could give a warning to people, like an attack is coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that Muslims in Bosanski Samac were not armed.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They were insufficiently, inadequately armed, compared to the others who had everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. In paragraph 14, you say that about a month before the 17th of April when, as you say, a conflict occurred in Bosanski Samac, you and the SDA organised guards and patrols; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose they were unarmed because you say yourself that you did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: By that time, the MUP was already divided. Serbs manned police stations in Serb villages and Croats in Croat villages. We had guards at entry points into the town, and the guards had some weapons when they rode in vehicles, but they didn't display them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this conclusion you drew about the possible attack of Serbs against the town is based on the fact that every weekend complete Serb families left the town, and they explained it to their neighbours by saying that they feared an attack.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fact is that Serb families were afraid from a -- of an attack from Croatia, and based on that you draw a conclusion that they -- that there could have been a Serb attack.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every Thursday or Friday, Serbs would leave the town, but they were saying that the JNA would attack -- the Serbs would attack, not Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you decided to put up guards and patrols because Serb families had left the town fearing a Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, we were not afraid of the local Serbs, we were afraid of those special units that were coming from Serbia. We were afraid of the JNA. We would never wage war with the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement you mentioned only precisely local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: As leaving the town, not as a possible source of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned them as setting up this 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the 4th Detachment and many people who used to be in the 4th Detachment were later disenchanted because they could see where it was going. These Specials were coming into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Just tell me now, in this annex to your statement, there are excerpts from interviews which you say in paragraph 62 and 63 were given under duress, and you were told prior to those interviews that you should say that nobody had beaten you and the police were treating you well.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, when I was interviewed by the Novi Sad TV station, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, so you were told to say that nobody beat you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you never said that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: There was a break during the questioning, and then there was this break and then Stevan Todorovic said to me I would be asked whether I had been beaten and I should answer that I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that aside now, that they asked you to say that you were not beaten. Is it correct what you said then about the arming of Muslims in Bosanski Samac? Let me be quite specific: Is it true that Alija Fitozovic, on behalf of the Municipal Board of the SDA, had direct contact with Slavonski Brod from where he obtained weapons from members of the SDA? This is in line 20 of your interview, on page 0089624.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had permanent contacts. I doubt that he had permanent contacts, but he went from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And obtained weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Obtained the ammunition I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is the other claim right, also on page 624 in lines 22 and 23, that in these activities he was assisted by a certain Rifat Atic, nicknamed Ice, and Izet Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's these three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You stated then that the question of arming within the SDA constantly burdened your meetings at lower levels and higher levels; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. People simply felt threatened, frightened. Nobody had any weapons whereas others did. Present, we're going to get killed, we're going to get slaughtered, and you have no weapons, and you haven't got any money, and you simply don't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, is it true that precisely as president you told Alija Fitozovic and Izet Izetbegovic to take care of arming and that the two of them had all contacts in that respect as well as coordination with the top echelons of the party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask them to take care of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it right that with regard to arming, Izet Izetbegovic contacted a person who you knew then as Senaid [phoen], and this was Senaid Memic [phoen]. This is 0089265. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what you said then, that the first quantity of arms delivered to Bosanski Samac contained 30 automatic rifles and five pistols? On page 625.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You mean what was obtained from Memic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These weapons were brought from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Memic, Senaid Memic, the person you mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And soon after that, another delivery followed, including 50 automatic rifles and two mortars; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the very eve of the attack on Samac. This was placed at the Territorial Defence depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning what was involved. And today you claim in your statement -- you said awhile ago you didn't have any weapons. All of this was delivered at the beginning of 1992, January, February; right? So all of four months prior to what happened in April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, March, April, or perhaps even February, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And we heard from you that as for the reported attack of Serbs on town, you found out about this in mid-March, a month prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what people said, but we didn't know exactly when the town would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even before that it is not contested that you obtained weapons as early as the beginning of the year and that you were preparing for something, attack or defence. What? Which one of the two?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Defence, what else? There were so few of us there. We simply tried to survive, if possible. There were only 8 per cent of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Izetbegovic and Fitozovic obtained different calibres of ammunition, a large number of explosives? This is what you said during your interview.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You keep repeating one and the same thing, you see. I mean, you've talked about this ammunition and these grenades so many times. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the dates are different. Also 100 kilogrammes of explosives that was intended to carry out various actions in the territory of the municipality; is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if there were 100 kilogrammes. Possibly. I never saw this. And I think that this entire quantity was taken away from Fitozovic afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a certain quantity was found, as it says here on ERN 623 in lines 10 to 21, in the house of Alija Fitozovic and the other one at the SDA, or rather, the Islamic Community's presence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think it only could have been found in the house of Alija Fitozovic, not at SDA premises. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading what it says here on this page that ends with number 623.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to read the numbers slowly, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard that. You're asked to read out numbers more slowly for the interpreters. Would the legal officer come up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00892623. That is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So please look at this document according to which Mr. Fitozovic obtained explosives from Slavonski Brod, 100 kilogrammes were found in his apartment, or, rather, part of it was found in his apartment and another part at the SDA premises, or, rather, the premises of the Islamic Community.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters again note that they do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it could not have been found at the premises of the Islamic Community, only at his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just read out what it says here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the same occasion when explosives were found, that also a schematic of the transmission lines that had already been blown up was found in his possession, as well as a schematic of those that were about to be blown up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, he worked for the power company, so perhaps he had these different diagrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I would now like to remind you of the fact that towards the very end of this interview with the journalist you were asked whether there was the possibility of the Serbs and Muslims continuing to live together normally, whether you had any advice to give to either one of the two ethnic groups. I assume that you remember that. I will jog your memory in terms of what you answered. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see, first of all, whether the witness remembers what you're claiming or asking him about. Do you remember this, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what you answered, I am quoting you: "I am so pleased that you're asking me this. Had you asked me this before all these events, perhaps the answer would have been similar, but at any rate, all those who pursue the policy of the party should experience certain things directly and see what all the consequences of this suffering are and then it would be far easier for them to reach some kind of agreement. We in Bosnia think along those lines, that we have to live together. There will be these three republics, or I don't know, these three cantons or whatever it is called in formal terms, but yet again we will have to cooperate. We live in a Bosnian Yugoslav territory. These borders that will exist among cantons, that will exist among states, will, probably after five or ten years, be put down altogether. So why are we killing each other over that? I believe that any Bosnia, regardless of whether it is independent, sovereign, international recognised, is not worth any sacrifices and victims. So all of those who represent the Muslim people in that way would have to bear this in mind, because if an ethnic group that accounts for one-third of the population of Bosnia cannot be taken slave, and it is not all right to enslave anyone regardless of whether they are one fifth or whatever. If somebody wants to be a Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, go ahead, but nobody can be forced to do anything." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. And you know under which circumstances this statement was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Nobody probably suggested to you to give this kind of broader political explanation regarding the territory of Yugoslavia, that it was pointless to get killed for some kind of independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's for sure as far as this unified area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Yugoslavia, the European Union, well, that's for sure, with borders disappearing and co-existence in spite of differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what the former Yugoslavia was.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you decided to secede from it and to create these borders. Isn't that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. And we could have a long discussion about that now but we strove for Yugoslavia, for a community of equal peoples. Unfortunately, the Serbs and Croats, especially the politicians who represented the Serb people, did not wish to have that. They wanted to have a domination of the Serbs, and that led to the disintegration of Yugoslavia, which is where we all felt comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was the best solution for all the Yugoslav peoples; isn't that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was the best solution, but regrettably, they could not keep it. It's not only the Bosniaks who could have preserved Yugoslavia, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. This is your own position. Nobody imposed it upon you what I quoted to you just now.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, statements that are taken in police stations where you're beaten, where they do all these things to you, and then before this statement Crni comes to you and says, "You are going to go and make a statement and then you're going to say that you are giving instructions how someone is going to shoot from Slavonia," whatever, so consciously or unconsciously, you try to gear your statement towards the person who is compelling you to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you should be in that position and then you will see what kind of freedom you have in terms of giving a statement. There is no freedom there whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17, you see that about 20 days prior to the attack, the alleged attack on Bosanski Samac, in front of the coffee bar of Rifat Atic, members of the 4th Detachment, one Serb and two Muslims, shot in the air and that on that occasion two persons were wounded. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They shot in the direction of the coffee bar, and that's when the police came up. Thinking that they were shooting at them, they responded, they returned fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these two persons that you refer to were Muslims, Nijaz Ramusovic, nicknamed Tota, and a certain Mersad, were precisely members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And fire was opened at them for no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a reason, because they were the first to shoot, you see. They were the first to shoot. And then the police responded and the two of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were members of the 4th Detachment, although they are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They were members of the 4th Detachment, and this was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You know very well and I assume they both Ramusovic and this Mersud --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Mersad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't know the exact name, so of course you can correct me. According to the information I received, they did not open fire. They were ambushed because they were members of this 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's not right. That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They did the shooting, and it was after their shooting that the police shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that those who shot at them, who wounded them, were Adis Izetbegovic and Sead Srna, members of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those two members of the reserve police force shot at these two Muslims. Both sides were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, both were Muslims. And these two policemen were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but this Adis Izetbegovic is also a relative of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He is Izet Izetbegovic's son and therefore a distant relative of President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the mentioned Muslims, you certainly know the names of Fadil Topcagic, Avdo Duhic [phoen] Fikret Sajakovic [phoen], Kadir Korolic, Fehir Kapetanovic, Alija Palesovic [phoen], Sali Sadinovic [phoen], Ibro Ibrolic [phoen], Aslo Bajaktarevic [phoen] Ramo Bajaktarevic [phoen], Dzemal Jasenica [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't reel off a whole series of names like that. He won't be able to possibly answer. What is the question? In what connection should he know these names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The connection is that these Muslims who shot at those two Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment that took care of the safety and security of the municipality, that they had proclaimed them traitors, Chetnik vojvodas, things like that; is that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The persons whose names you read out were members of the 4th Detachment, the 4th Detachment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these men who shot at these people, did they proclaim them to be traitors and Chetnik vojvodas?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, not probably those two who did the shooting, but these people who were in the 4th Detachment were labelled that way, that they were collaborators of the JNA, that they were Chetnik vojvodas. Well, it depended on the position that various people held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I did not even read out the entire list because Mr. May interrupted me, but I assume that you know all these people by name and that they were all members of the 4th Detachment, and they were labelled as being traitors because they cooperated with the JNA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know most of them, and that is how the public viewed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
