utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 12th of April, 1992, Alija Izetbegovic ordered an all-out attack against JNA barracks in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 13th of April, a day later, the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mato Nujic, issued an order to the TO staff of the municipality to establish a unit?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's in accordance with the law, to establish a unit of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that on the 16th of April, commander of the TO staff, Marko Bozanovic, informed the republican staff in Sarajevo that on the 15th of April in Bosanski Samac, a Municipal Staff was established with about 1.800 military conscripts, Croats and Muslims only?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were only Muslims and Croats. I think there were Serbs there too and whether that was the figure, what he exactly wrote in the letter, I don't know. I assume that he simply provided information about the establishment of the staff, how many soldiers were involved and what the ethnic composition was. But at any rate, among them there were Serbs. To a lesser extent, but at any rate, they accounted for the proportionate number in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tihic, is it true that on the 16th and 17th of April, Croatian armed formations attempted to cross the river across the Sava River -- the bridge across the Sava River and launch an attack on Bosanski Samac together with those Croat units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three persons were killed in these attacks. Please refresh your memory. The 16th and the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. On these dates, Specials from Serbia attacked. The JNA and the Serbian Territorial Defence. It was they who attacked Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you take these Specials from Serbia from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They landed in JNA helicopters from Batkusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They were Red Berets, and the JNA brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from what you know, the JNA brought them.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. A client who came to see me in my office told me that. The JNA brought Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about those people killed in the attack when Croatian armed formations tried to cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Armed formations from Croatia did not try to cross the bridge, and when Samac was attacked, from what I know, these members of the special units killed one Serb person by mistake. Only one person was killed. Maybe even three. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know they were killed by mistake, not during the attack. Is it true that on the 18th of April, a new attack was launched --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He knows no such thing. You continually assist your view of something or other. What we're hearing is not your view but the witness's account. That is what matters, not your views. So we'll get on better if you ask your question, accept the answer for the time being, and then move on and not continually answer with the -- argue with the witnesses and make tendentious points. Now, let's hurry up. Time is short.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, don't argue. Stop arguing. Just get on with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm doing, but you don't seem to be paying attention to the fact that I'm asking questions about different dates. First I asked about the 16th and the 17th, and he said it was not true, then I asked him about the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the camp on the 18th. I didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about an attack on a column of women and children from Trnje in the direction of Prud?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I was in detained in the camp then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You heard his answer; he was in the camp. You should pay attention to it and we'll get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will follow the days as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all, Mr. Tihic, about the fact that from Croatia 108th, 124th and 139th Brigade of the ZNG were transferred across the river?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I would know if it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know about this first thing I asked because you were in the camp. You should know about the second thing.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I would have known if so many brigades had crossed over and came -- come to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you find anything about it after you were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about the presence of these brigades in this area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know they were in Orasje, Derventa, Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All that is in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are they all armed forces of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: These units, as you said, were units of the HVO, of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know nothing about any units of the Republic of Croatia present in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In that period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let us come back to this 4th Detachment. These Muslims that I enumerated to you and you confirmed they were considered as traitors and so on, were they members of the TO or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They were members of the JNA, because the 4th Detachment was formally, legally, and in reality part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So despite this order not to join the JNA, they were members of the JNA rather than the Territorial Defence. Very well, Mr. Tihic. In paragraph 16, you say that on the 16th of April, a joint meeting was held of all presidents of parties so as to decide who would defend which part of the city in the event of attack by Croatian armed forces probably coming from the other side of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, not in the event of attack by Croatian forces. We were just talking about possible attacks. They could have come from the Serbian side, from the JNA, or the Croatian side, and the 4th Detachment was afraid from -- afraid of an attack from the Croatian side, so we told them, you patrol the bank of the Sava River. We, on the other hand, were afraid of an attack from Serbian villages, and we said we would patrol the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "The night before Samac was attacked Bozanovic, Fitizovic, Zaric, and the presidents of all parties held a meeting to decide who would defend which part of the city in case of an attack. Muslims and Croats did not think that Croatian armed forces were going to attack, but the Serbs thought it might happen."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We were all there, and that was our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago that already in mid-March you knew that Serbs would attack Bosanski Samac. And now you hold this meeting and you don't know anything for sure and you are bargaining and guessing where an attack might come from and how to defend the town.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Milosevic, we simply assumed there could be various options, but we also believed at the same time that it would not happen, and Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, all of us sat down together. And if those Specials and the JNA had not come, we would never have started fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say a moment ago that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic - and I'm using the terms you used - tried to rise above it all and to treat the Croat, the Serb, and the Muslim sides equally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what he said, but in reality he distributed weapons only to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that even before the 17th of April there were constant armed provocations by members of the 108th and 129th Brigade of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It did not take place in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true Mato Nujic, president of the Municipal Assembly, and Mato Matarevic [phoen] told you personally about the joint plan in the event of an attack by the ZNG, the HOS, the Croatian armed forces, and the HVO against Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't told about it nor would I have ever agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You quote in another paragraph, 22, that Arkan attacked the police station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You know what, we called all these Specials by one name. We didn't distinguish between Arkan's men, the Grey Wolves, or other units. But it's true that Specials, member of special units, attacked the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you mention Arkan, but according to my information that was gathered by my associates, Arkan was never present in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I meant his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What units are you talking about? He only had a small group of volunteers, he didn't have any units.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's how they held themselves out, Arkan's men. How large the unit was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, during all these events, did you ever see Arkan anywhere in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you saw and you know that there was a number of volunteers who were active in Samac, but I don't know on what basis you link them with Arkan or the Red Berets, so could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You see, as far as the Red Berets are concerned, I already explained how they arrived in Samac on JNA helicopters, and they wore appropriate patches and insignia. And I know Arkan's men because they were in the camp, they beat us, they forced us to sing songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Samac. And they forced us to sing songs about Arkan's Tigers. I don't know how many there were. You couldn't talk normally to them, you couldn't look them in the eyes. You had to keep your head down, you were beaten all the time, you had to sing songs about Arkan's Tigers. Whether they were five or 50, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the reason why I'm asking, because according to the information gathered for me by my associates, Arkan had never been in Bosanski Samac. But let us go on through your testimony. Soon after these events in April, you were arrested, and you were detained in the police station in Samac after these events on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In the headquarters of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the headquarters of the TO?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It was in the same street. The police station faced the headquarters of the TO and I was detained at different times in both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29, the same afternoon, over the local radio you made an appeal to Muslims to stop fighting, and after that, one soldier told you you were free to go home.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You know what actually happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about what is written in paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It's true that I gave a statement. I was interrogated by this member of a special unit from Serbia who used the Ekavian dialect, who made me make that statement on the radio and to appeal on Muslims, although they never shot on anybody, they only shot in the air, to spread fear around town, and I had to say what he told me to say. I don't know what his name was, Bailji [phoen] or something. He was from Serbia. He interrogated me and he asked me to say this on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you are speaking about volunteers, do you, Mr. Tihic, have any idea how many volunteers from Serbia, from the area of Raska or Sandzak, how many thousands were in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there were any -- in fact, I don't think there were any from Sandzak directly. There were some people who had moved from Sandzak to Bosnia-Herzegovina and resided there for a while, but if you're talking about people who came directly from Sandzak to join the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was hardly possible because that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under occupation. It was not possible to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim there were no volunteers from Sandzak in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, no particular volunteers who were registered as such or had their own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about a special unit. Were they present in your forces?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It would have been difficult for them to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first place. If there were any, there could not have been many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even the commander of your Main Staff was Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, he first was employed by the JNA, then came to Bosnia from Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he comes from? Is he from Serbia, from Prijepolje? Did he ever live in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He may be originally from Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he do his military service in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he didn't even do his military service in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. Now, this second part of the question you didn't really answer. After that statement, after that appeal you made over the radio, the soldier told you you were free to go home.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, when you heard the shooting outside the building, you did not want to go out, because you were afraid of getting shot, and they could say that you got shot while trying to escape.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, because when they were taking me to the police station, Stevan Todorovic whispered something into the ear of this policeman, something that I thought might have been, "Liquidate him." So when they told me to go, they were standing behind me with automatic weapons, and I thought it was the perfect occasion to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only quoting you. You said in principle it was on a voluntary basis that you asked to return to the police station.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't want to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what you say is, "In principle, I did it on a voluntary basis." But if they were the kind of people that you say they were, doesn't it occur to you they could have killed you in the police station, if they had wanted to, or in any other place if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They also could have killed me in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that prove, Mr. Tihic, that they didn't want to kill you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't prove that, because, you see, I had only arrived at the police station and they took me immediately to the Samac radio station. I didn't know what was going on at the time in the police station, that there were 50 people already detained who were being beaten and tortured. I thought the police station was safe and that's why I wanted to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you explained that. You spent ten days in the police station in Samac. Is that correct, Mr. Tihic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you the first time. And then you say that in that interview you had given to the journalist from the Borba newspaper you were beaten by some people who were not local Serbs but members of paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's what they wrote, members of paramilitary units. They were members of special units from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they paramilitary units or not, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They could not have been paramilitary units with the kind of weapons they had and the kind of uniforms they wore. In my opinion, they were special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is -- in your opinion, were they part of the local TO?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, they were independent; they acted on their own, they didn't listen to anybody. They had some sort of command elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If they didn't listen to anybody, then they could not have been part of the regular forces.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: But they had the support of the regular forces in terms of weapons and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. Although you claim in your statement that both in Batajnica and in Sremska Mitrovica you were beaten and mistreated by members of the JNA, which I must confess sounds very improbable to me, you said in your interview given to the Borba newspaper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to suggest that, the witness must have a chance to answer. The accused says it sounds improbable to him that you were beaten by members of the JNA in Batajnica and Sremska Mitrovica, Mr. Tihic. Do you want to answer that? Were you beaten by members of that organisation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was beaten by members of the JNA. Mr. Milosevic, I found that incredible too, that children, soldiers were beating me just because my name was Sulejman. Regular soldiers. Believe me, I was not the only person there. There were so many of us. And also reservists were there too and regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. You say in your interview to Borba: "Instead of a few hours, they kept me in prison for ten days. I don't have to point out to you specifically what I went through there. They beat me, they threatened me." I'm quoting your interview to Borba, a Belgrade daily newspaper, and this newspaper published what you said. So you say: "They beat me, they threatened me, but I must say that these were not local Serbs but members of some Serb paramilitary units that had quite simply occupied this area. The local Serbs in Bosanski Samac and in Brcko even provided me with food and tried to console me, saying everything would end well." And now this is the point: "But only when they handed me over to the JNA I knew for sure that my life had been saved." Are these your words?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So only when they handed you over to the JNA you were certain that your life had been saved.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: At that time, I still believed -- we still believed in the JNA, because, out there, anybody could come and kill you, just like that, without being held responsible. And when you were with the JNA, then at least your name was registered. And when we were in Brcko with the JNA, the JNA did not let them beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your life had been saved, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: But I'm just telling you what the atmosphere was like, the members of these special units and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this reflected your position, which was a realistic position. Only when you were handed over to the JNA, you knew that your life had been saved; is that right? Now, speaking of the prison and the conditions in Sremska Mitrovica, you say: "We read that this prison and other prisons are being called concentration camps, but there is not even a C here from camp. It's not as if we were living at home with our families, but things can't be better in times like these. After all, my friends and I are not real prisoners here. We are hostages. We are being treated better than we thought we'd be treated, but nobody can be happy if they are behind such walls." Are these your words, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether these are my words, but we were beaten in Mitrovica after breakfast, after lunch, and after dinner, every single time. I was never beaten more in my life than in Mitrovica. And also, our lives were threatened. But perhaps my life was in greater danger elsewhere, but I was never beaten as much as I was beaten in Mitrovica. You know, in three or four months the JNA was transformed to such a great extent. The JNA in Brcko that did not allow us to be beaten to the JNA in Mitrovica where they beat us, where they forced us to sing Chetnik songs and all these things, all these things were so bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there as a prisoner under the control of the JNA in Sremska Mitrovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a camp, a concentration camp within the prison, the former prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was, as you say, something that was under JNA control, but then you say here that there is not even the initial C of the word camp there let alone it being a full-fledged camp.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's not true. Read my statement. When the warden of the camp took me out and said that I would be interviewed by Sky News, that I would be interviewed for Borba and he wanted us to say that nobody beat us, that it was clean and tidy, that we could go out for walks, that we had sufficient food. And of course if you want to be exchanged, that's what you have to say. And of course I had to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At one point in your statement, you corroborate the claims made in that interview, and in other parts of the statement you say that you were interviewed under duress, and you say that you were beaten in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was beaten. Everybody was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you gave this interview on the 12th -- 12th or 13th August, 1993 by the BBC.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think it was Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But already on the 13th of August this interview was published in the Belgrade daily Borba. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, this was about two or three days before I was to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph, you say that the new warden, a JNA lieutenant, told you to say that they had not beaten you, that meals and walks and medical assistance were invariably provided, and that you could say that Arkan's men beat you in the prison in Bosanski Samac and that you should say to the Red Cross that you do not wish to return to Bosnia but that you wish to remain in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him, "Well, can I say that I was beaten in Bosnia?" And he said, "Well, whichever way you want. You can say it, but you know I would not advise you to do that. Your sister lives in Rijeka. You know they can come to Rijeka too."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do have this interview of yours, Mr. Tihic. Since you said that he told you all of these things concerning meals, walks, medical care, show me a place in your interview where you refer to these meals, walks, medical care, or show me where you say in this interview that you wished to remain in Serbia and things like that. Everything that you said that he ordered you to state is not contained in your interview. So you did not state any of this, and you claim that he ordered you to state that and that, under duress, you stated what he ordered you to state. In this interview, there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: We did have to state that and now it's a different story whether somebody actually wrote this down or published it or televised it, but that is what we were told to do, and that is what we said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. Well, didn't you speak actually contrary to these alleged instructions given by this lieutenant? Didn't you state the opposite in the interview, that you were dying to go back home to your family, and that you're appealing to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they should not forget you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's what they asked us to do too. I even had to write a letter to President Izetbegovic to tell him to release some soldiers so that they would release us from the prison in Mitrovica and in Morina in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what are you being asked to say, that you wanted to stay in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or that you should ask to go back home to your family, which is what the interview says. What were you asked to do? You cannot have both.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They asked me to state that I want to stay in Serbia, that I do not wish to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did not state that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they told you to state that you had sufficient food and that you went out for walks and that you had medical care, and they did not ask you that you wanted to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's what you stated.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's what I stated, and I also said what I said about the hygiene and walks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us this in the interview, where it says so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was written down in the interview but that's what they asked me. That's what they were afraid of the most, you see, that we should not talk about the beatings, and of course you would be crazy to talk about the beatings because after the journalists left, you had to stay with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am saying the exact opposite. This is 00516378 and 00516379. Those are the ERN numbers. Please bear that in mind. Thank you, Mr. Tihic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much, but it seems to me that we have a problem here. It is true that that document that was referred to a moment ago by Mr. Groome had been disclosed in March without the indication of the name, and we found out only today the name of the person who provided the document, namely his notes. So in practical terms, Mr. Milosevic was unable until today to review this document and see if he had anything to challenge regarding the document. I believe it is my duty to point this out, and I believe he should be given the opportunity to review this document maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, time is against us in all this. This document was disclosed. What we can do is this: He will have the opportunity to review the document. If there is some substantial matter which would require further cross-examination, we may have to ask the witness to come back, but I think it would be better if we could finish the witness's evidence today rather than waste further time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a suggestion. The witness's plane leaves tomorrow afternoon. Could I ask that Mr. Milosevic be required to read that material this evening and advise the Court tomorrow morning first thing if he -- if there is a substantial matter, and perhaps it could be dealt with while Mr. Tihic is still in the country on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, first of all, I should like to ask you to explain to the Honourable Judges a couple of things from your statement from February 1995. I don't think Mr. Milosevic dealt with it. Would you please look at paragraph 4 of that statement. Have you found this? It is tab 2. You say here in paragraph 4: "Before the 1990 elections, the SDS, SDA, and HDZ had good relations. We all wanted to take away power from the communists." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to assume power from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you said a moment ago, and as it says in your first statement, you were a member of the League of Communists until 1989, and then just a year later you worked for toppling the communists.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, all these new parties were mainly made up of former members of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You also say that you supported one another. But regarding the future of Yugoslavia, there were always differences in the approaches of the SDS on one hand and HDZ and SDA, that is, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you added then: "The SDS and the HDZ believed in a confederation supporting independent republics while the SDS wanted a strong federation and a whole Yugoslavia." You said a moment ago that the best solution for Muslims was Yugoslavia, where everybody felt comfortable. How do you explain then that already in 1990 your party supported independence for the republics?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: We wanted either some sort of federation or stronger confederation. In 1990, we were still far from any discussions or declarations of independence. We were talking about some sort of loose federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I did quote you a moment ago, and I'm asking you to explain to the Judges. When you were giving this statement, did you also adjust your views, as stated here, which seem to be contrary to what you said today? In other words, even then when you thought that Yugoslavia was the best solution, did you have to adjust that opinion because you were giving this statement to the investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. Even today whenever you are giving a statement, you are asked to be concise. You are asked not to go into details, and you cannot really state all your views in full. These are broad political issues that are presented here only briefly. If you give me an opportunity to explain how I saw the possibility for independent republics, what kind of federation, et cetera, et cetera, I could do that. I thought then and I think now that Yugoslavia should be a union of equitable peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 2 of this much broader statement. Twenty-two, paragraph 22, from year 1994. You said somewhere in the middle of that paragraph -- but before I quote you, I have to say that a moment ago, you particularly emphasised that if the JNA had not interfered, none of what happened would have happened.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say in the middle of this paragraph,: "Safet Hadzialijagic, nicknamed Pop, member of the SDA, came to see me and said that the JNA should offer to be a buffer zone between Arkan's men and the townspeople, but I was opposed to that." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Safet Hadzialijagic called me on the phone and presented this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were against it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, by that time Samac had already been attacked and I told him I had to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But then you say here that Ibrahim Salkic came, said that Nikolic had called him, and said that the JNA was prepared to give guarantees if weapons were surrendered.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, if you had to choose between the JNA or Arkan's men, JNA seems better if you are already under attack and people are being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 54. You say here: "In the course of the evening on the 26th or the 27th of April, at approximately 10.00 p.m., two lorries came to pick up about 50 of us who were supposed to be taken to Brcko. There were no Arkan's men in the street." And you go on to say: "The prisoners were afraid that Arkan's soldiers would appear all of a sudden and prevent the JNA from taking them to Brcko." Does that mean that JNA was actually protecting these prisoners precisely from something that could have happened if the JNA had not been there? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, we were so badly beaten by those Specials that we were hardly breathing. And when the JNA came at Zaric's request, they actually saved us; otherwise, we would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 56 you say: "The army doctor gave me an injection and put something on his face to make him recover consciousness. While we were imprisoned at Brcko we received medical treatment, and the JNA mainly protected us."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more topic. You speak of Sremska Mitrovica as a concentration camp. You were a lawyer and a judge in those times and you know full well that this prison in Sremska Mitrovica is actually a prison for the detention of criminals, and it holds at all times several thousand -- several thousands of people who were convicted of crimes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It was established during the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and part of it was a concentration camp. One part which was fenced in and separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the Red Cross came to visit you only on the 22nd of June. Prior to that date, did anyone beat you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, regularly, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just two minor topics. Paragraph 103. When they were taking you back in that convoy of 1.500 prisoners, you were stopped in Serbian villages and they allowed villagers, you state here, to get into buses and beat you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say the convoy was accompanied by a large number of press representatives, at some point even the Red Cross was present, and the UNPROFOR men who told you to keep your heads down lest you be hit by a sniper. Is it possible that it all happened in the presence of the UNPROFOR, the Red Cross and everyone else, and the press, that they allowed villagers to get into buses and beat you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: The journalists came only to the venue of exchange in Nemetin. As for this road, which was over 100 kilometres long across Vojvodina, there were no journalists there. But even in Nemetin, where there were journalists and the Red Cross representatives, they still beat us. And one major approached this Montenegrin man who was on the bus and told him, "What are you doing, you dumb fool? We didn't beat them for several days so that they wouldn't look black and blue."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. If you were not a lawyer, I wouldn't be asking you this, but since you are, I have to ask you this: You said in paragraph 106: "A full month after all of this happened, when I came home I was afraid to fall asleep. I went to see a doctor for three broken ribs and my four front teeth that had been broken." Please, since you were an attorney by occupation, did you get an X-ray of those broken ribs, and especially did you take a photo of those four missing teeth, and did you turn these photographs over to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to see the doctor, X-rays were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you do you have a medical document, a certificate, for these broken ribs and missing teeth?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I think I submitted them when I testified in the Samac trial. There were X-rays or perhaps doctor's findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are these teeth still missing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They were broken, and I had fillings done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, Mr. Milosevic has expressed some doubt about the statement that you made to the television reporters from Novi Sad. I want to ask you about your treatment briefly before you had given that statement on Novi Sad television, and if you're able to answer the questions simply by yes or no, that may save us a bit of time. Prior to giving that statement to Novi Sad, so that the Court can better understand your state of mind, had you had a gun, pistol, placed in your mouth? I'm referring to paragraph 44 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Just before I made my statement, no one put a pistol in my mouth, but Djordjevic did threaten me, and he asked that I be brought down there and that I should be careful about what I say. And Stevan Todorovic also threatened me and asked me to say that I was never beaten. And all of this happened in front of the journalist who heard all of this. What kind of journalist is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the time immediately prior to the statement but in your treatment leading up to the time you gave the statement. Can you -- as a result of your beatings --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were beatings, there was mistreatment, there were threats to shoot with that white pistol with nickel put against my temple and then also putting a pistol in my mouth and threatening to shoot. Of course I was afraid. All these same people were there again, and I was in that kind of atmosphere, and that's when I was supposed to give a statement. And they threatened me, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to this time, as a result of the beatings, had you sustained injuries to your kidneys, as described in paragraph 54 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had sustained these injuries. I urinated blood. And the late commander of the police station in Samac, even when these Specials were not there, he would bring in a doctor to see me, or they'd bring me lemonade or whatever, because the two of us had known each other for a long time, and we lived in the same town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your description of your treatment by the JNA, it appears that different members of the JNA treated you differently at different times and in different places. I want to now focus on your treatment by the JNA while you were in Serbia in the period between May and August. During that period of time, did you witness prisoners being beaten by JNA personnel using brass knuckles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them using brass knuckles. They were beating them with that, a group that came in from Bosanski Brod. And usually the prisoner would sit on the floor, handcuffed, and they would hit him on the back, on the head. Aljo even died. He could no longer take it. He started urinating, he didn't know what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were some of the men forced to perform sexual acts upon each other by members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were. There were situations like that too. They made an American have sex with a soldier from Croatia, Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during the two-and-a-half-month period that you were incarcerated in Serbia in the custody of the JNA, were you ever charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Never. I was never formally interviewed. I never signed a statement. Once this major from Batajnica took me for an interrogation, but there was never a record of that. Also, there were never any charges brought against me, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, that concludes your evidence, at least as far as today is concerned. Would you be kind enough to have yourself available, to be available tomorrow morning in case there are some more questions. But if not, thank you for coming to the Tribunal, that does conclude your evidence apart from the matter which I have mentioned, and therefore, you're free to go, but if you would be available tomorrow morning. One administrative matter I'm going to deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and it's this: We will admit, under Rule 89(F), the statement of Mr. Dean Manning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise a brief procedural matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the testimony or anticipated testimony of General Clark. Pursuant to the Chamber's order, the amici and the accused will notify the American government either through the Office of the Prosecutor or directly whether they wish to ask additional questions or go into additional topics on their examination. I have a query from the American government this morning, saying that they have not heard from either the accused or the amici. It may take several days to process such request and they are asking me to convey or just remind all the parties concerned that it will in fact take a few days and if there are requests coming, if they can be notified of such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're aware of that. It's just, with the volume of work, it's been impossible to get so far ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, with that in mind, perhaps you would concentrate on it. Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock testimony morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
